items.followUp: Name two types of enzyme used in biological detergents and state which stains they remove.

rubric.description: Names proteases and links them to removing protein stains.

rubric.why: Lipases break down fats and oils.
rubric.description: Names a second enzyme and links it to removing its stain type.
rubric.how: Award for a correct enzyme-use pairing distinct from the first credited point.

modelAnswer: Proteases in biological detergents break down protein stains such as blood or egg.
Lipases break down fat and oil stains.

items.followUp: Define aerobic respiration and write its balanced chemical equation.

rubric.why: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy.
rubric.description: Defines aerobic respiration as glucose breakdown using oxygen and releasing energy.
rubric.how: Award for the key idea of glucose breakdown with oxygen releasing energy.

rubric.why: The balanced equation shows glucose and oxygen producing carbon dioxide, water and energy.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation for aerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Award for a correctly balanced equation or its correct word equation.

modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy.

items.followUp: State the products of alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.

rubric.why: Alcoholic fermentation converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide, usually through yeast action in the absence of oxygen.
rubric.description: Defines alcoholic fermentation and identifies its products.
rubric.how: Award for the anaerobic conversion to ethanol and carbon dioxide.

rubric.why: Lactic acid fermentation converts glucose into lactic acid without oxygen.
rubric.description: Defines lactic acid fermentation and identifies its product.
rubric.how: Award for the conversion to lactic acid, typically in muscles or bacteria.

modelAnswer: Alcoholic fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose by yeast to form ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Lactic acid fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose to form lactic acid, for example in muscle cells or some bacteria.

rubric.why: Bio-energetics concerns energy in living systems.
rubric.description: Defines bio-energetics as the study of energy relations or transformations in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award for linking the study of energy to living organisms.

modelAnswer: Bio-energetics is the study of energy relationships and energy transformations in living organisms.

items.followUp: Distinguish between saturated and unsaturated fatty acids and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Saturated fatty acids have no carbon-carbon double bonds; unsaturated fatty acids have one or more.
rubric.description: Distinguishes the two types by the presence or absence of carbon-carbon double bonds.
rubric.how: Award for a correct contrast between saturated and unsaturated fatty acids.

rubric.why: Palmitic or stearic acid is saturated; oleic or linoleic acid is unsaturated.
rubric.description: Gives an appropriate example of each type.
rubric.how: Award when examples correctly represent both categories.

modelAnswer: A saturated fatty acid has no carbon-carbon double bonds; an unsaturated fatty acid has one or more carbon-carbon double bonds.
Palmitic acid is an example of a saturated fatty acid, while oleic acid is an example of an unsaturated fatty acid.

items.followUp: Define macronutrients and name two examples needed by plants.

rubric.why: Macronutrients are nutrients required in relatively large amounts.
rubric.description: Defines macronutrients by the large quantity required.
rubric.how: Award for stating that they are needed in large amounts.

rubric.why: Examples of plant macronutrients include nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
rubric.description: Names two valid examples of macronutrients.
rubric.how: Award for any two correct examples.

modelAnswer: Macronutrients are nutrients required by organisms, especially plants, in relatively large amounts.
Examples of plant macronutrients include nitrogen and phosphorus.

items.followUp: Explain four other careers related to Biology, apart from medicine.

rubric.why: Biological knowledge is used to improve crops and farming practices.
rubric.description: Explains agriculture as a biology-related career.
rubric.how: Award for linking biology with crop production or farming.

rubric.why: Biology supports the breeding, care and management of animals.
rubric.description: Explains animal husbandry or veterinary work as a biology-related career.
rubric.how: Award for a career explanation involving animal health, care or breeding.

rubric.why: Biology is used in fish breeding, production and fisheries management.
rubric.description: Explains fisheries or aquaculture as a biology-related career.
rubric.how: Award for linking the career with fish or aquatic organisms.

rubric.why: Forestry applies biology to forests and trees; other biological careers include biotechnology and environmental biology.
rubric.how: Award for a relevant career and its biological application.

modelAnswer: Agriculture: biologists help improve crops and develop better farming practices.
Animal husbandry: biological knowledge is used to breed, feed and care for livestock.
Fisheries: biologists help breed fish and manage fish production and aquatic resources.
Forestry: knowledge of biology is used to manage forests and protect trees and wildlife.

items.followUp: Describe how temperature and substrate concentration affect the rate of enzyme action.

rubric.why: Increasing temperature raises enzyme activity up to an optimum; excessive heat denatures the enzyme.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of rising temperature, including the optimum or denaturation.
rubric.how: Award for increased activity up to the optimum or loss of activity due to denaturation.

rubric.why: Low temperatures slow enzyme action, while the optimum gives the greatest activity.
rubric.description: Adds the effect of low temperature or identifies optimum temperature as giving maximum activity.
rubric.how: Award for a correct additional temperature effect.

rubric.why: Increasing substrate concentration increases the reaction rate while enzyme active sites are available.
rubric.description: Explains that added substrate initially increases enzyme activity.
rubric.how: Award for linking increased substrate concentration to a faster reaction.

rubric.why: The rate levels off once all enzyme active sites are occupied.
rubric.description: Explains that the rate stops increasing when enzymes become saturated.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the active sites become occupied and the reaction rate levels off.

modelAnswer: As temperature rises, enzyme activity increases until it reaches an optimum temperature.
Above the optimum, the enzyme denatures and its activity falls; low temperatures slow the reaction.
As substrate concentration increases, the reaction rate increases while enzyme active sites are available.
The rate eventually levels off when all active sites are occupied and the enzymes are saturated.
